text:
Dear Dr. Vance,

Thank you for seeing Arthur, a 7-year-old boy who first presented around 3 years of age with recurrent bruising and spontaneous epistaxis. He lives with his parents, is currently attending second grade, and is on no chronic medications. His family history is negative for bleeding diatheses or consanguinity.

On physical examination, his vital signs, cardiovascular exam, and chest auscultation were entirely normal. Inspection of his head revealed a striking silvery metallic tint to his scalp hair. Abdominal examination demonstrated marked enlargement of both the liver and spleen, with each extending several centimeters beneath their respective costal margins. There was no peripheral lymph node enlargement detected. His developmental milestones have all been met appropriately, and there is no evidence of global developmental delay.

Recent hematology revealed a depressed total white blood cell count of 2.6 x 10^9/L, low hemoglobin at 8.6 g/dL, and a reduced circulating platelet count of 52 x 10^9/L. Evaluation of the peripheral blood smear demonstrated massive, abnormally large granules within the cytoplasm of his neutrophils. Platelet aggregometry showed defective, blunted aggregation responses following stimulation with collagen, arachidonate, and ristocetin. Subsequent electron microscopy identified a marked paucity of dense storage granules in his platelets.

Given this constellation of hematologic and physical findings, I would greatly appreciate your specialized assessment and advice regarding the appropriate diagnostic direction and clinical care.

Sincerely,

Dr. Julian Howard
